entries.title: Trump Administration Delays Iowa Lead Detonation to Wednesday
entries.summary: The administration said it would be investigating the contractor that runs the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant for how it handled the lead explosives.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is again delaying the planned detonation of lead explosives in Iowa, this time to Wednesday, after widespread outcry from communities furious that they were not sufficiently warned about the possibility of a toxic lead plume.

The White House is expected to investigate how dangerous lead azide explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant were allowed to deteriorate to the point that they needed to be detonated, as well as launch a probe into the contractor that manages the plant, a source familiar with the situation told The Washington Sun.

American Ordnance, the contractor responsible for managing the explosives at the plant, and its inspectors discovered the deterioration in the lead in March 2026, according to EPA permitting documents and Army communications reviewed by The Sun.

The White House, led by President Donald Trump’s new chief of staff Stephen Miller, convened a team of agency leaders alongside the Homeland Security Council and National Security Council over the past 48 hours to discuss why the explosives had to be detonated and how to mitigate potential risks to the public, the source said. Senior White House officials only became aware of the issue Thursday, even though the Army has been planning how to deal with the problem for about six months.

The source requested anonymity to describe details of the unfolding situation.

The Army had already delayed its planned detonation of 68 barrels of degrading lead azide to Monday from the Friday original schedule, warning that was the latest possible date before the risks of an uncontrolled explosion became too great.

Sunday night, the Army posted to X that the detonation would occur Wednesday “to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced.”

“The Army and our interagency partners have been working around the clock to safeguard all Americans in the region,” the Army said in the post. “Additional details on this situation will be forthcoming. The health and safety of all Americans has and always will be our first priority.”

The administration said in court filings that cold temperatures will dramatically increase the chances that the lead azide — which has been degrading for months — could spontaneously explode, sparking a public panic over a lead dust plume spreading in the air above the Middletown plant.

The Army insisted in court filings over the weekend that the explosion could not be delayed past Tuesday, at the latest, because of the risks. While a federal court temporarily blocked the EPA permit authorizing the explosion, Justice Department attorneys warned that the Army would proceed with the detonation plan regardless of the judge’s ruling because it deemed the situation to be an emergency that merited operating without a permit.

The Army also revealed in court filings that it previously considered and then abandoned a plan to neutralize the lead azide with chemicals, warning that it would be too dangerous for anyone to try opening the lids of the barrels holding the lead in order to do the chemical treatment.

“So this was truly a choice between controlled or uncontrolled detonation,” the source familiar with the situation said. Now the discussion has moved on to how the government can put “as many mitigation measures in place as possible to protect the public.”

Public anxiety about the dangers of a lead plume escalated over the weekend with news of the pending explosion. An Army official familiar with the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive matter, told The Sun that the “exposure for the unmitigated worst case scenario here would be roughly equivalent to living in Los Angeles or New York City for three days in 1985.” Leaded gasoline was still in use at that time, making ambient lead exposure relatively quite high compared to today.

No amount of lead is safe to ingest, according to public health experts. Lead is a toxin that is especially dangerous to children, who are more sensitive to brain and nerve system damage.

Iowa officials, including Gov. Kim Reynolds, said they were only made aware of the Army’s plans to detonate the explosive one week ago, when the Army published maps showing a possible lead dust plume stretching across southeastern Iowa and into Illinois.

The Army increased the risk of an uncontrolled explosion in preparation for the original detonation date by removing the heavy metal bunker doors protecting the lead azide. Now those doors cannot be replaced, and the explosive is more vulnerable to swings in cold temperatures, The Sun previously reported.

“Unfavorable winds could increase the dispersion of lead dust into the community,” according to a DOJ filing in court. “An uncontrolled deportation of nearly five tons of primary explosive would endanger soldiers, contractors, and the surrounding communities, all without many of the protective measures meant to minimize the risks from the blast — harm that cannot be undone.”

Iowa environmental groups on Thursday sued the EPA — which permitted the detonation — in an effort to try to delay the scheduled explosion. The Army is not party to the suit.
entries.author: Anna Kramer, Jasmine Wright

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: ‘One of Our Own’
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 23, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: A memorial at VIDA, a loss at Audi Field and a daunting challenge at Northwest Stadium. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 7/10. A quick shower is possible but this is the last warm-ish day of the week. Enjoy it before temperatures tumble. Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

Nearly two weeks after a deadly shooting left the Logan Circle community reeling, the streets outside of VIDA Fitness filled on Saturday afternoon for a memorial to honor victims.

Family members of James Stuart, the Metropole building manager killed inside the gym by resident Dr. Matt Lambert, sobbed and held each other in grief. Stuart’s niece, Aby Stocker, told reporters that although her family “was going through it,” they appreciated remembering her Uncle J’s bright spirit and sense of humor.

“I think of his laugh,” she said. “I hear his laugh a lot.”

Andrew Wilkinson came out to honor the friendship he had with Stuart. Although the two were “a little catty” initially, they became inseparable. Wilkinson remembered asking to stay with Stuart as he underwent chemotherapy. “Being my best friend, he didn't hesitate,” he said.

The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports that several attendees emphasized the need for gun control. Constance Freeman, a gun violence survivor and leader of D.C.’s chapter of Moms Demand Action, came to honor MDA member and shooting victim Susan Hamerski.

“That one of our own was injured, it's important for us to stand up and show up for her — as we do all victims of gun violence,” she said.

VIDA Fitness founder and CEO David von Storch expects the gym to reopen Tuesday.

VIDA memorial (5712x4284, AR: 1.33)




DEEP DIVE

Spirits were low Saturday, after the Washington Spirit’s NWSL championship match against the Kansas City Current ended in a heartbreaking 2-1 loss, The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri reports.

“Obviously, this one hurts way worse than any of the other ones,” Trinity Rodman told reporters. “I don’t think you even have words in the moment. It’s too fresh.”

It was the team’s third straight championship loss, but fans had hoped this year would be different. It was the Spirit’s first championship played at home, in front of a hungry, sold-out crowd at Audi Field. The surge of fans marching to the stadium from The Wharf ahead of the game felt like a preemptive victory parade. Those who couldn’t score tickets crowded into neighboring bars, ready to flood the streets for a postgame celebration.

“This is the time, this is the night,” said one superfan, waiting to enter Audi.

They never got that moment. Still, supporters felt some consolation in just what a spectacle the night had been, and all in the service of women’s sports, The Sun’s Zara Norman reports.

“We used to play at a high school soccerplex in Maryland, now we sell out a stadium, like, every week,” said one fan, a D.C. resident of 25 years and season ticket holder. “I love seeing it.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

A push to bring a 10-cent refundable deposit for bottles and cans to D.C. is dead. The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports that the bottle-deposit bill introduced by Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau won’t be advancing this year, largely because of a multimillion-dollar lobbying blitz against it by the beverage industry and growing concerns within the D.C. Council over whether it would increase costs for retailers and consumers.

Some 10 states have bottle deposit programs in place; advocates say they increase recycling rates and could cut down on trash that ends up in D.C.-area rivers. Nadeau, who is leaving office in January, says she hopes a future council will take up the bill again.

The future of Montessori education in D.C. Public Schools is uncertain after the system allowed the accreditation for three schools to expire Friday. Shamira reports that J.C. Nalle and Langdon elementary schools and Capitol Hill Montessori at Logan will no longer be affiliated with the Association Montessori Internationale, the organization that sets international standards for many Montessori schools.

The decision comes after several parents have expressed surprise and concern over a changing curriculum. In a letter sent to parents days, DCPS said it plans to pursue accreditation from the American Montessori Society — another major Montessori organization — in a process that could take several years.

Out of the shadows: D.C. shadow Senator Ankit Jain is running for an at-large seat on the D.C. Council, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports. Jain could retain his position as shadow senator while simultaneously serving on the council.

Monumental setback: A federal judge indefinitely suspended President Donald Trump’s plans to construct a 250-foot memorial arch in Arlington while a lawsuit brought by the county board plays out, Kendall reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

A Princeton doctoral student was arrested by ICE at Reagan National Airport last week as she prepared to fly back from a conference, NBC4 reports. The student, Eva Yi Xie, is being held at a detention center in Bowling Green.





FROM MARYLAND

The butterfly symbol that Maryland residents with hidden disabilities can feature on their state-issued IDs to have smoother interactions with first responders will be offered to students in Montgomery County Public Schools starting in January, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports.





TRIVIA


How many teams were in the NWSL when the Spirit first joined in 2013?

  1. 8
  2. 10
  3. 12
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

Dan Quinn AP - 26318716818509 (5070x3380, AR: 1.50)
The Commanders have their work cut out for them tonight. Hosting the Bengals on “Monday Night Football,” Washington will be tasked with finding a way to stop one of the league’s best offenses. But The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson reports that the team is undaunted, firm in its belief that they can compete with Joe Burrow and company.

“You can’t play this game, this position, having fear in your heart,” defensive back Amik Robertson said. “You respect the opponent, but you also go out there and play fearless.”

A lot of attention has been paid to Wizards rookie AJ Dybantsa this season, but what about the rest of the team’s young core? As Washington struggles to get this season off the ground, The Sun’s Alex Schiffer checked in with scouts around the league to see how they view players like Alex Sarr, Kyshawn George and Tre Johnson.

What to Watch Today

NFL: Commanders vs. Bengals, 8:15 p.m. (ESPN)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Gaby Morera Di Núbila.

entries.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang After Trump’s Urging
entries.summary: The company said its board of directors unanimously voted to reinstate him.
entries.content:
Jensen Huang is once again the president and CEO of Nvidia after the computer chip giant’s board of directors unanimously voted to reinstate him, Nvidia announced Monday.

Huang stepped down from the position less than two weeks ago after news broke that he had an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China. Huang reportedly also had an affair with two other employees at Nvidia, which is underpinning the United States’ current artificial intelligence buildout.

The company said in a statement that it “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

After suggesting that former Apple head Tim Cook take the role, President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social Sunday night that he hoped the board would rehire Huang. Huang also put out feelers in a statement following his resignation, telling the board he would come back if they would have him.

Trump said in a Truth Social post on Monday that the board had made “the correct and proper decision” and that the government “has no reason to believe” Huang’s return “poses any risk to National Security.”

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American economy,” Trump wrote, adding that the government does not have any evidence of “unlawful conduct” from Huang.

Nvidia, however, should continue its internal investigation on export control compliance, Trump wrote.

The Department of Justice announced last week that it has been investigating cloud computing company Megaspeed — once led by Alice Huang, who was reportedly in touch with China’s Ministry of State Security during her affair with Jensen Huang. The Department of Commerce launched its investigation in 2024 after noticing “potential sensitive semiconductor diversion.”

“We have to see where the buck stops,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CBS’ “Face the Nation” Sunday. “Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?”

Nvidia said it formed a new committee “comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks.”

Jensen Huang said in a statement that he is “honored to return.”

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” he said.

It’s not the first time a major technology executive has returned from a short-lived exile. OpenAI’s board of directors ousted Sam Altman in November 2023 — in part over allegedly misleading the board — only for Altman to return less than a week later.
entries.author: Kyle Chouinard

entries.title: Two States Sue Musk’s SpaceX Over Sexualized Grok Image Creation
entries.summary: Virginia and Oregon contend the company violated consumer protection laws by failing to prevent users from creating and viewing nonconsensual AI-generated sexual content.
entries.content:
Virginia and Oregon filed state consumer protection lawsuits Monday against SpaceX Super Intelligence Corporation, alleging the Elon Musk-owned technology company failed to prevent the creation and promotion of sexualized images of children and adults.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield said in their press releases that SpaceX’s online safety policies are misleading and haven’t adequately protected users from AI-generated sexualized images through its AI-assistant, Grok.

“This lawsuit is about seeking justice for the millions of Virginians who maintain accounts on X and were misled by the company’s false reassurances that their data and images would be safe on the platform,” Jones said in a press release.

“When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Jones said. “Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”

The Democratic attorneys general argued in their lawsuits that SpaceX’s policies violate consumer protection laws. Virginia’s complaint alleged that SpaceX declined to adopt “industry-standard safeguards.”

The same morning of the lawsuit filings, X’s safety account posted on the platform to emphasize its dedication to online safety, specifically mentioning Grok’s AI image and video generation feature.

“When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement,” the post said. “Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

Musk’s xAI and Grok introduced “spicy mode” in July 2025, a setting that allowed users to generate nude and sexualized content, and then paywalled the service in January. When Musk purchased X in 2022, he said in an online post that eliminating child exploitation content from the platform was “priority #1.”

Virginia’s complaint argued SpaceX and Musk’s public statements about their policies are “false, misleading, or deceptive.”

“In truth, Defendants had not implemented or enforced policies and safeguards to identify, remove, and police such content,” the complaint says of SpaceX’s policies. “To the contrary, Defendants intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM, NCII, and nonconsensual sexualized images.”

In its complaint, Virginia said the state conducted an investigation into Grok and its capacity to generate sexual images before filing, finding that the platform’s safeguards failed to consistently block requests and allowed users to circumvent blocks.

“The Commonwealth’s own investigation using a test account revealed that shortly before the filing of this Complaint, Grok remained capable of generating non-consensual sexualized images of real, identifiable people from ordinary photographs that a user uploads,” the complaint says.

Both of the lawsuits also accuse SpaceX of benefiting from sexual image generation features. The Virginia complaint alleged that Grok’s daily downloads grew by 72% in January, just after the company introduced AI-generated sexual content.

Virginia and Oregon’s attorneys general are both seeking financial damages for the alleged safety failures.

The debate over online safety has been growing for years and heated up in August, when social media giant Meta agreed to a $17.1 billion settlement with 47 states and D.C. over youth mental health and the platform’s addictive features.

In early November, 45 attorneys general — including from Virginia and Oregon — called on Congress to pass the Senate version of the Kids Online Safety Act, which would require online platforms to exercise reasonable care in preventing online harms for children.

Congress has tried to regulate social media and technology companies’ online safety policies over the past several years, but has not been able to pass legislation. Last week, at a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hearing, Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) again pushed Congress to pass bills like the Stop CSAM Act, which would combat the creation and promotion of child sexual abuse materials online.
entries.author: Ellie Fivas

entries.title: Ethics Committee Says Jimmy Gomez Made Unwanted Sexual Contact With a House Staffer
entries.summary: Gomez’s actions “could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse (more commonly referred to as sexual assault),” the committee found.
entries.content:
The House Ethics Committee released a report on Monday saying that Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez of California made “unwelcome sexual advances and sexual contact toward a House staffer.”

The committee spoke to 10 witnesses while conducting its investigation. A woman identified only as Witness 1 told committee staff that “she had more than one physical encounter with Representative Gomez and she did not consider them consensual,” per the report. The woman was a House staffer but did not work directly for Gomez, the report says. She told the committee she stopped working on the Hill in part because of what Gomez did.

“The Committee also notes that Representative Gomez’s behavior towards Witness 1 could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse (more commonly referred to as sexual assault)” and could violate local Washington, D.C., laws, the report says.

Under the current rules of the House of Representatives, members are prohibited from having romantic or sexual relationships with any employee directly under their supervision.

Such a prohibition does not exist for relationships between lawmakers and staffers, including interns, who work in other congressional offices. But lawmakers are prohibited from engaging “in unwelcome sexual advances or conduct” toward any House employee.

The committee said Gomez had unwanted sexual contact with the woman at an unnamed member of Congress’ birthday party in 2024, and a few months later in Gomez’s office, where the woman described him as being “pretty forceful.”

The Ethics Committee highlighted the power imbalance between a member and someone who has to interact with them for work.

“The reality of that power dynamic is further evidenced by Witness 1’s testimony that she did not want Representative Gomez ‘to feel upset in any way,’ that she was concerned that any incident would be construed as ‘the woman’s fault,’ and she was ‘afraid that I was going to get in trouble at work,’” the report says.

The committee added: “Despite Representative Gomez’s characterizations of these incidents as isolated and private, for Witness 1 they were anything but. Instead, Representative Gomez’s conduct caused a traumatic and ongoing chain of interactions for Witness 1 which, combined with a broader culture of sexual misconduct on the Hill, drove her from government service.”

Gomez’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but he has previously denied any wrongdoing. He told the committee that the woman “did not say no, she did not push me away,” but ultimately, the committee found that his testimony “does not come close to establishing her consent to the sexual contact.”

Gomez lost the race for his seat to Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres.

Because he did not win reelection, the committee said “there is not enough time for it to pursue an adequate House sanction.” However, the panel said the report needed to be released “so that the House is aware of Representative Gomez’s misconduct and so that the House may determine, in its judgment, whether to sanction Representative Gomez.”

Throughout multiple interviews, Witness 1 told the committee the “toxic and predatory culture on the Hill that she experienced.”

“I think it’s something that’s definitely happened to me a lot on the Hill where, like, people get handsy; they touch me or, like — you know, and so my reaction is just to always sort of, like, back off, like, make sure no one saw that because then I don’t want anybody else to think that’s okay,” the woman told the committee.

The committee said that “this is not acceptable.”
entries.author: Oriana González

entries.title: The House’s New AI Caucus Has Big Ambitions — And Divisions
entries.summary: The group’s founders want the caucus to be a response team for AI incident information and to help get legislation on Trump’s desk.
entries.content:
The bipartisan group of lawmakers behind the House’s new artificial intelligence caucus wants to become a “rapid response”-style team for Congress “when new incidents crop up,” Rep. George Whitesides (D-California), who co-chairs the caucus, told The Washington Sun.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Virginia), another of the caucus' three co-chairs, is aiming higher. He said he hopes members can get an AI safety bill on the president's desk in the first half of 2027.

The House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus launched last week with 26 members — 19 Democrats and seven Republicans — in hopes of responding to growing concerns around an uncontrollable advancement of AI. Where Congress’ existing AI caucus, which Beyer also co-chairs, has been “educational,” this one will be about working on policy, the Democrat said.

“We want to be a bipartisan team working together to get something that can actually pass,” Beyer told The Sun.

The group’s formation shows Congress’ widespread interest in putting up guardrails around AI. But it also highlights the challenges ahead. Despite a growing consensus that something needs to be done, there are major divisions even within the newly formed caucus on how to proceed.

Nearly a dozen of the new caucus members have introduced AI bills of their own since July — some with conflicting positions.

The FRONTIER Act, introduced in July by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-California) and Lori Trahan (D-Massachusetts), both founding members of the caucus, would block states from adding their own rules in three areas: catastrophic-risk transparency, third-party auditing and incident reporting. Trahan is now rewriting it to set a federal floor that states could build on.

Reps. Sara Jacobs (D-California), a founding member, and Celeste Maloy (R-Utah) released an outline with Beyer for a potential bill that would also set a federal floor, taking the same approach Trahan is now pursuing.

Meanwhile, Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), a founding member who also chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus, wrote a bill with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) to ban superintelligent AI outright — a position Republicans are unlikely to sign on to.

Republican leaders have framed AI advancement as a race with China. House Speaker Mike Johnson rejected calls to pause AI development, warning it could slow American innovation.

"Whatever the downsides of AI are, they get magnified a thousand times if China surpasses the U.S. in its AI technology advancement," Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas), the third co-chair of the caucus, said in a statement.

Moran said incident reporting, model control and testing “can all be done without slowing deployment."

Moran and Rep. Ted Lieu (D-California), also a founding member of the caucus, introduced a bill in July that would require companies to maintain shutdown capabilities and allow the government to order it in emergency cases.

The caucus itself probably won’t write bills, Beyer said. And its members have acknowledged they may not agree on major questions in the AI regulatory fight, like whether federal rules should preempt state laws.

"I think we'll have different views probably in the caucus on that issue," Whitesides said of preemption. He said states can make "a really thoughtful and useful contribution," pointing to California.

But, he said there’s a “whole set of things that I think there’s wide agreement on,” including required incident reporting, export controls, whistleblower protections, model transparency and more funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation.

Whitesides, NASA's former chief of staff and Virgin Galactic's former CEO, said he wants the caucus to be a go-between for the engineers building AI and the lawmakers writing rules for it.

"I think the greatest risk is no regulation," he said. "I view regulation as really the critical foundation for the benefits of AI to flourish."

No matter the disagreements, the caucus will work under new leadership in January, when Democrats take the House majority.

"One of the frustrations I've had is that Speaker Johnson has not wanted to move any AI legislation at all," Beyer said. He said incoming leadership is "going to be much more interested in trying to keep AI safe."

Some in the group have also joined the effort in lobbying Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries to form an AI select committee.

Moran said he would “fully support an AI select committee in the 120th [Congress]."

Lieu and Rep. Bill Foster (D-Illinois) pitched Jeffries on such a panel in September. Beyer said he has joined the push but added that committees which already have AI jurisdiction “probably won't be excited to hand this off to somebody else.”

"We don't absolutely have to have a select committee," Beyer said. "It might be that our little caucus might serve the same function of getting together people across party lines to sort out differences."

Beyer expects the caucus to first meet in the first or second week of December, between votes to keep the government open and pass the National Defense Authorization Act. Senators from both parties filed amendments to that bill this summer to tighten controls on AI chips and set rules for how spy agencies use AI. Neither chamber has voted on them.

"Right now is the time to make sure that we are talking and working across the aisle on these tough issues — to stay focused on policy and shun the desire to make this issue hyper-political," Moran said.
entries.author: Ayah Ali-Ahmad
